claims.statement: Harry Allen was arrested and put under £1,000 bonds, which ended the planned fight with Joe Goss.
The court held that training for a prize-fight was not a violation of the laws of the State, and so discharged the arrested man.
Tom Allen was arrested in Cleveland on Wednesday, charged with violating the prize-fighting laws. The name is lost in the OCR text (printed as ', the pazibst,'); the headline names Allen.
After the McCoole fight, Tom Allen sued to recover his stake money.
Tom Allen was arrested in Ohio and required to sign a bond not to fight in that state.
Tom Allen was arrested in Cincinnati on 14 May 1869 on a charge of training for a prize fight in the State of Ohio.
Tom Allen gave bonds of $500 (printed as £500) not to fight in Ohio within a year, and was released.
Tom Allen was arrested in Cincinnati, Ohio, but was released on a bond not to violate Ohio's laws and went back to training.
Billy Carroll offered $100 to any responsible man who would say he had offered to bribe McKinney; Carroll, Thurston, B. Riley and James Stewart swore counter-affidavits.
The money taken on the boat stayed with the men who took charge of it under a legal process; the stakes were understood not to have been given up.
Referee Val McKinney swore that Sherman Thurston and Billy Carroll offered to let him name his price to decide the fight for them.
A sheriff and his deputies broke up the Allen-Goss fight, and the fighters fled to an adjoining county.
John Williams sued Tom Kehoe and Mike McCoole, the stakeholders of a $30 bet on the proposed Allen-Gallagher fight, and the court gave judgment for the defendants.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole compromised their claims to the excursion money from their 1869 fight; McCoole took $1,232.50 and Allen $1,000.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole went to law over the stakes of their 1869 fight, and the stakes were still undecided.
Tom Allen was arrested on the steamboat Belle Ida and taken to the Central police station on November 1, 1870.
Daniel B. Stephens petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, saying Tom Allen was held illegally in the calaboose with no charge against him.
The habeas corpus petition for Tom Allen was presented to Judge Stewart of the court of criminal correction.
A writ of attachment was ordered against Chief of Police James McDonough for contempt of court in not producing Tom Allen.
Chief James McDonough surrendered Tom Allen to the court, which discharged him; no charges were made against Allen.
The planned Allen and Gallagher fight, set for Tuesday, was spoiled by police interference.
Allen's lawyer, Mr. Voullaire, said a report that Allen intended to sue the city for false imprisonment was untrue.
The fight was arranged in secret so the police would not be told, and was held early in the morning.
Tom Allen was in Mace's party at Wyandotte when Sheriff William Holcomb of Wyandotte County tried to capture them; they were not taken.
A rumour in Pleasant Hill had Tom Allen, supposedly with Jem Mace, in town, and the sheriff and deputies hunted for him.
The coroner's jury found that Nelson Adams died from a pistol wound caused by the accidental discharge of a pistol in Tom Allen's hands at Allen's saloon, 417 Washington avenue, on May 20, 1872.
After the shooting Tom Allen ran for a physician and called the police.
Tom Allen's fights with Mike McCoole near St. Louis were indirectly responsible for the Missouri boxing statute of 1873, which made prize fighting a felony.
Joseph P. Moore said Allen came down and struck and kicked him, laying him up for twelve days in the City Hospital.
Witnesses said Allen knocked Joseph P. Moore down and kicked him in the head in the saloon skirmish.
Tom Allen was on trial in the Court of Criminal Correction.
Tom Allen was charged with assault to kill after Joseph P. Moore complained of being beaten and kicked in Allen's saloon.
The judge discharged Tom Allen on the evidence.
Police Captain Burgess and about a dozen policemen were present to testify to Allen's good character, but the judge said it was unnecessary.
Tom Allen was a witness for the defense in the Mollie McCoole case in Police Court on Saturday morning.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole were arrested by detectives on Sunday night, 21 September 1873.
Tom Allen was arrested at a temporary snuggery, the 'Hunter's Retreat' near Jefferson Barracks, while McCoole was arrested at his training quarters.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole were released from the Four Courts on bail of $1,000 each, to keep the peace in Missouri for three months.
Tom Allen was arrested on the morning after McCoole's arrest at his training quarters.

Judge Colvin of the Court of Criminal Correction accepted $1,000 bonds from Tom Allen and Mike McCoole to keep the peace in Missouri for three months; John Whelan and William Brown signed the bonds for Allen and McCoole.
Maj. Jones offered Tom Allen as a witness to prove that Mike McCoole was too sick to appear in James Scott's $900 debt suit in Judge Knight's court, St. Louis; the case was continued.

A Madison County, Illinois, writ ordered the sheriff to take Tom Allen and others to the circuit court at Edwardsville to answer an indictment for prize-fighting in the Allen-McCoole fight, returnable Monday, Nov. 3.
John Renshaw of St. Clair County swore an affidavit that Tom Allen and Ben Hogan were about to fight in Illinois, and asked for warrants against them and their backers.
Illinois Gov. Beveridge sent Col. E. L. Higgins, adjutant general, to East St. Louis with a hundred stands of arms to prevent the Allen-Hogan fight.
Gov. Beveridge of Illinois had issued requisitions for Tom Allen, Mike McCoole and others engaged in the September prize-fight.
Allen said he could not fight in Missouri because of bonds.
Tom Allen and Arthur Chambers were arrested by St. Louis detectives on arrival from Kansas City, on an Illinois requisition for the prize fight with Mike McCoole.
Tom Allen and Arthur Chambers were taken to the Four Courts in St. Louis and held there without bail.
Tom Allen put up $3,000 in greenbacks as collateral for the Illinois bail bond that freed Arthur Chambers.
Police Chief McDonough intended to push the Wash Home case against Tom Allen and his associates, and would not use Ben Hogan as a witness.
Tom Allen, Johnnie Smith, Sam Smith and Jim Eagan were discharged in Police Court over their Sunday chase after Ben Hogan, without making a defense.
Tom Allen said his Police Court cases over the chase after Hogan had been dismissed on evidence that morning.
The Missouri governor signed the bill suppressing prize-fighting, which the Republic said dimmed Tom Allen's hopes in Missouri.
